% --------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Vertical balance and the frame ending (G2, G6, G9)
%   \FrameTop          first token of every frame body: stretch above the content
%   body / figure -> \Interp -> \SourceNote -> \Backups (or \BackTo, \BackToTwo)
% The content block is centred between the title bar and the note/button rows:
% \FrameTop and the glue before the note block (or, without a note, before the
% buttons) share the free space. The note block sits on the row just above the
% buttons, which sit on the last row above the footer (PI directive 8).
% Every \SourceNote is followed by \Backups, \BackTo or \BackToTwo in the same
% frame (lint_deck.py checks this).
% --------------------------------------------------------------------------
% \FrameTop takes back 0.15 cm of beamer's fixed 0.2 cm [t] top skip, so the block
% sits optically centred (measured: equal stretch alone left the top gap 0.27 cm
% larger than the bottom gap on every slide).
\newif\ifdeckSrc
\newcommand{\FrameTop}{\global\deckSrcfalse\vskip -0.15cm plus 1filll\relax}
% Final fixer (7 Oct 2026): at 8.0 pt most notes run to 2 lines. To make room, the button row is set on the
% button font's own leading (\DeckBtnRow: the buttons stay on the same last row; only the dead glue above
% them goes), \Interp sits 0.06 cm under the figure (was 0.15), and the note keeps a fixed 0.06 cm from the
% text above it, so it never touches the \Interp lines on a full slide. The note is \raggedright (not
% ragged2e's \RaggedRight, whose 2em stretch let an unbreakable 'Benjamini--Hochberg' overrun the line).
\newcommand{\SourceNote}[1]{\par\vskip 0.06cm plus 1filll\relax
  {\color{Muted}\FsNote\raggedright #1\par}\vspace{0.12cm}\global\deckSrctrue}
\newcommand{\DeckNavGlue}{\par\ifdeckSrc\else\vskip 0pt plus 1filll\relax\fi\global\deckSrcfalse}
\newcommand{\Interp}[1]{\par\vspace{0.06cm}{\centering\color{Ink}\FsBody #1\par}}
\newcommand{\BL}[2]{\hyperlink{#1}{\beamergotobutton{#2}}\hspace{0.15cm}\ignorespaces}
\newcommand{\DeckBtnRow}{\usebeamerfont{button}\baselineskip=8.4pt\relax}
\newcommand{\Backups}[1]{\DeckNavGlue{\DeckBtnRow\noindent\hfill#1\unskip\par}}
% Return links. In the short build (main_short.tex) a backup may point back to
% a main slide that the short path omits; the link then goes to the backup
% index instead, so every link resolves in both builds. The footer carries
% the "Backup index" link on every backup.
\makeatletter
\providecommand{\ShortLabels}{}
\newcommand{\bt@target}{}
\newcommand{\bt@set}[1]{%
  \ifdefined\ShortPath
    \@expandtwoargs\in@{,#1,}{,\ShortLabels,}%
    \ifin@\def\bt@target{#1}\else\def\bt@target{B-index}\fi
  \else\def\bt@target{#1}\fi}
\newcommand{\BackTo}[2]{%
  \DeckNavGlue{\DeckBtnRow\noindent\hfill
  \bt@set{#1}\hyperlink{\bt@target}{\beamerreturnbutton{#2}}\par}}
\newcommand{\BackToTwo}[4]{%
  \DeckNavGlue{\DeckBtnRow\noindent\hfill
  \bt@set{#1}\hyperlink{\bt@target}{\beamerreturnbutton{#2}}%
  \hspace{0.15cm}\bt@set{#3}\hyperlink{\bt@target}{\beamerreturnbutton{#4}}\par}}
\makeatother

% Note numbers: [S1] 1,020 PMEs; [S2] 397 people involved in PME hiring or manpower decisions; [S5, S6] mirrored choices on a common menu
% Removed from the round-4 note, pending the PI: "the analysis and options are the SMU team's" - a governance fact, see B-governance
\note{[Short path] Colleagues from MOM, NTUC and SNEF: the question for Singapore is no longer whether flexible work exists, but which arrangements can retain PMEs while remaining workable for firms.
In this joint study with SNEF, 1,020 PMEs and 397 people involved in PME hiring or manpower decisions made mirrored choices on a common menu of arrangements. % [S1, S2, S5]
The results point to common ground, a role-dependent case, and arrangements that need testing before scaling.
Values in per cent of pay are a measuring rod, not a proposal to lower pay.
The findings are preliminary; we end with a decision for the partners.
[Timing: 130 words a minute plus 15 seconds a slide. Short path, 15 slides, target 17 to 18 minutes: Title, Motivation, Question, Framework, Design, PMEs, Why PMEs, Employers, Where, Meet, Compressed week, Barriers, Options, Conclusion, Thank you. The full deck adds Literature, Data, Estimation, Descriptive, Groups, Robustness, Discussion and Limits.]}

% ==========================================================================
% 2. MOTIVATION   [short path]
% ==========================================================================
% Directive 1: the figure is large, centred and dominant (F_motivation drawn at true size 14.0 x 5.0 cm, FigC).
% Directive 3: the mandated title and caption state the policy problem, fit; no bullet column.
\begin{frame}[t,label=M-motivation]{Flexible work is mainstream; the policy problem is fit}
  % F_motivation: establishments with 25+ staff, private plus the public sector, offering at least one scheduled
  % FWA, June 2008-2025 [P4s, P4]; title "Establishments (25+ staff, incl. public sector)", fixer pass 7 Oct 2026;
  % labelled points 28.1 in 2008, 52.7 in 2019, 90.5 in 2021, 68.1 in 2023, 72.7 in 2024 [P4s, P4]; 66.4 in 2025, MOM
  % Supplementary Survey, no causal reading [P4, P4s]; Guidelines in effect 1 Dec 2024 [P1]
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_motivation}
  \Interp{Aggregate provision does not show whether firms offer the arrangements workers value.}
  % Polish pass, 7 Oct 2026 (DESIGN_PLAN s2 W1, G5/G6): F_motivation is redrawn at 14.0 x 5.0 cm with no footnote
  % line; its footnote moves here verbatim as the slide's source line, so the budget is figure 5.0 cm + two-line
  % caption + one 7.5 pt source line + buttons (compiled deck is the fit authority; slack_check.py).
  % Source line: [P4s] MRSD time series released 30 Jun 2026, establishments with 25+ staff; [P4] MOM gives no
  % reason for the 2025 fall; [P4s] 77.5 incl. newer types, 2024
  \SourceNote{\textbf{Source:} MRSD, MOM (Jun 2026).} % [P4s, P4]
  \Backups{\BL{B-laboursupply}{Labour supply} \BL{B-guidelines}{Guidelines}}
\end{frame}
% Note numbers: [P4s] 28 in 2008, 73 in mid-2024, establishments with 25 or more staff, private plus public sector;
% [P4, P4s] 66 in 2025 and 68 in 2023, both MOM's odd-year Supplementary Survey; [P6] fewer working-age residents per senior, no number spoken
\note{[Short path] Flexible work is now mainstream. In 2008, 28 per cent of establishments with 25 or more staff offered a scheduled flexible arrangement; by mid-2024, 73 per cent did. % [P4s]
The 2025 reading, 66 per cent, comes from MOM's odd-year survey, which gave 68 in 2023; we do not read the change as an effect of the Guidelines. % [P4, P4s]
With fewer working-age residents per senior, keeping people in work matters more. [Detail: B-laboursupply.] % [P6]
But a firm offering one arrangement may not offer the one a worker values, or one the role can sustain.
So the partners' question is no longer how many firms offer flexibility, but which arrangements, for which roles, on what terms; MOM's surveys are well placed to track that.
That points to three open problems.}

% Note numbers: none spoken. Context only: [P1] the Guidelines set a process; [P2] no administrative request counts;
% [P3] MOM's need-request data, almost entirely pre-Guidelines, and MOM's frictions reading (spoken, no number; mom_ps-03);
% [D9, B6] our request item was partly misread and no why-not item exists; [R16, L1] the Polish two-sided study
\note{[Short path] The Guidelines already set a process for requests. MOM's own survey finds that few who need an arrangement ask formally, a gap MOM attributes to frictions rather than employer resistance. % [P3]
What remains open is fit, in three parts.
First, high overall provision can hide which arrangements are on offer, and whether they suit the worker and the role.
Second, few studies measure together how workers value each arrangement and how employers weigh it in hiring; a Polish study is one. % [R16, L1]
Third, career worries, unclear terms and the effort of job redesign can block arrangements that would suit both sides; reasons for not asking are rarely measured.
For the partners, the question is which arrangements to make easier to try now, which to tailor by role, which to test before scaling, and what information is missing.
We use a simple map. [Full deck: first, where this sits in the research.]}

\note{[Full deck only]
Flexible work is already common among the PMEs we surveyed: about seven in ten use at least one arrangement, and two in three use WFH. % [D1]
Staggered hours come next, at 27 per cent; the compressed week, job sharing and part-time are each used by only four to six per cent. % [D1]
On the employer side, 78 per cent of firms offer remote work to PMEs, but between about one in six and one in three also offer each of the other arrangements: flexible work is not only WFH. 60 per cent of firms call one to two WFH days typical for their PMEs. % [M16, D3]
These are our samples, not national rates.
More arrangements come through company policy than individual requests, so SNEF could share written FWA policy templates with member firms. % [D5x]
Next, the choice task that lets us put a price on each arrangement.}

We surveyed 1,020 PMEs and 397 people involved in PME hiring or manpower decisions, from unweighted online panels; the firms lean large. % [S1, S2, S3, S4]
Each PME chose six times between two job offers; each employer, between two equally qualified candidates. % [S5]
Here, offer A pays 10 per cent above the PME's own pay and B 10 per cent below, but B has one to two WFH days and a compressed week: the same hours over four longer days. % [S6b, S7]
Pay gaps were 17 to 33 per cent by design, so rankings are firmer than prices. % [S6, EB s9]
For employers, this is a hiring choice, not a reply to a request. % [S5; EB s9]
Now the results, starting with PMEs. [Full deck: ``Next, how we turn these choices into values.'']}

% [R13] employers picked the cheaper candidate only 57% of the time, a weak salary response
% [Q8] benchmark: candidate with a >20% turnover risk wins 33.6% (28-39, appended), the grey row of F_org_eqpay (bracketed cue, fixer pass)
% [D3] 62% of surveyed employers call 1-2 WFH days the typical PME arrangement (employer-02; MANDATE information/learning)
\note{[Short path] Now employers. These are hiring choices between two equally qualified candidates, not responses to a staff request. Each bar is the pay cut employers would require of a candidate who wants the arrangement, compared with an otherwise identical candidate. % [S2, S5]
A compressed-week candidate: about 7 per cent, not distinguishable from zero. One to two WFH days: about 20; three to four days, 36; fully remote, 49. % [R5, R1, R2, R3] appended
Because the pay gaps shown were 17 to 33 per cent, cuts above 33 go beyond what respondents saw: read them as a ranking, not a price. % [S6; EB s9]
Salary moved choices only weakly (the cheaper candidate won 58 per cent). % [R13]
Most surveyed firms already use hybrid work: 60 per cent call one to two WFH days typical for PMEs. So a hiring reservation may reflect role needs, uncertainty or a candidate signal, not simply opposition to hybrid work. % [D3]
SNEF and member firms could start pilots near the top of this ranking.
Put side by side, how far apart are the two sides?}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-meet]{The two sides' values meet only for the compressed week} % [s3b] 50% = no preference, read within each side only (Lead decision 3)
  % F_meet_r5 (fig_r5.py, 14.0 x 4.7 cm; integrator pass 7 Oct 2026: the header on one
  % line gives the slide 0.30 cm of slack): two visibly separate panels, each with its

  % fixer pass 7 Oct 2026 (mom_ps-09): one x-range per panel, PMEs 40-80 and employers 10-70, so the panels share
  % no ruler; footnote (editor-01): zones A-C are descriptive labels [Q16]; PMEs' remote vs own commute [M1];
  % header printed in the figure: "Compare each side with its own 50%; do not
  % compare distances across sides" (mandate, M-meet). Zone labels A/B/C inside are
  % descriptive labels [Q16]. Model-based equal-pay shares with 95% CIs:
  %   left, PMEs:       compressed week 58 (55-62) [Q5]; 1-2 WFH days 58 (55-62) [Q1];
  %                     3-4 WFH days 61 (57-64) [Q2]; fully remote 64 (61-68, vs own commute) [M1, Q3]
  %   right, employers (appended, n = 397): compressed week 47 (41-53) [Q5]; 1-2 WFH days 40 (35-45) [Q1];
  %                     3-4 WFH days 31 (26-36) [Q2]; fully remote 23 (18-28) [Q3]
  %   F_meet_r5 redrawn for the appended sample (fig_r5.py, 14 Oct 2026)
  % "1--2", "3--4 WFH days" are attribute levels [S7], not data values.
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_gap_m}
  % compressed-week wording: mandate "Evidence and language rules"; [Q5] 47% (41-53, appended) includes 50
  \Interp{Only for the compressed week do the two sides agree (about 7\% each).\\ For WFH, employers ask for 12 to 34 points more than PMEs would give up.}
  \SourceNote{Gap: pay cut employers require minus pay PMEs would give up, in points of pay, with 95\% intervals.}
  % Note = F_meet_r5's former footnote, verbatim (polish pass 7 Oct 2026): [s3b] equal-pay shares, 95% CIs;
  % [Q16] zones A-C are descriptive labels; [M1] PMEs' fully remote is measured against each PME's own commute.
  % [S1] 1,020 PMEs, 4-21 Aug 2026; [S2] 397 employer respondents (appended sample)
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Here the two sides sit on one scale: the pay PMEs would give up, and the pay cut employers would require, for each arrangement. The gap between them is the friction. % [E1-E7, R1-R7]
For the compressed week the two are about the same, 7 per cent each: no detectable gap. % [E5, R5]
For one to two WFH days, PMEs would give up 7 per cent and employers would require 20: a gap of about 12 points, and it depends on the role. For three to four days the gap is about 26 points, and for fully remote work about 34: the sides are far apart. These are indicative; employer cuts above 33 per cent go beyond the pay gaps shown. % [G2, G3, G4, S6]
SNEF and volunteer firms could test the compressed week first. So why is it rare? % implication (who could act) and transition to M-puzzle (short path)
[If asked: the zones are descriptive labels; the gap is employers' required cut minus PMEs' accepted cut, so positive means friction.]
Next, what do employers worry about, and does it change what they ask?}


% ==========================================================================
% 13. MECHANISMS: WHERE EMPLOYER RESERVATIONS SIT (association)   [short path]
% ==========================================================================
\begin{frame}[t,label=M-employer-barriers]{Employers name productivity, coordination and fairness}
  % F_fwa_challenge_m (scripts/fig_fwa_m.py): QID50 biggest challenge in offering FWAs, all 397 employers incl. Other
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_fwa_challenge_m}
  \Interp{Productivity, coordination and fairness are each named by about a quarter of employers.\\ Digital infrastructure and security matter much less (6\% each).}
  \Backups{\BL{B-org-view}{Employer view}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Asked for the biggest challenge in offering flexible arrangements, employers name productivity and output quality (24 per cent), team coordination (24) and fairness across roles (23). Managerial resistance or lack of trust follows (14). Digital infrastructure and security are named by 6 per cent each. % [B1, fwa_challenge]
The three leading items are statistically indistinguishable in this sample. The question asks for one challenge for FWAs in general, not for each arrangement, so it cannot say why a given arrangement, such as the compressed week, is offered by few firms. % [B1]
Next, does the pay cut employers ask for depend on where they need people on site, and on these concerns?}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-where]{On-site needs raise the WFH pay cut, not the others}
  % F_where_pres_m (scripts/fig_fwa_m.py from results_fwa/employer_splits.csv; scripts/fwa_employer_splits.py): pay cut employers would
  % require, all seven arrangements, by on-site presence need (137 firms: most PME roles need presence; 260: some or few). Fully interacted
  % conditional logit (group-specific pay slope); location p = .025, non-location (staggered, compressed, job sharing, part-time) p = .60.
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_where_pres_m}
  \Interp{Where most roles need on-site presence, employers ask for 28 to 49 points more for WFH.\\ The other arrangements show no such difference, yet few firms offer them. Early evidence only.}
  \Backups{\BL{B-why-org}{Tests}\BL{B-org-concerns}{Concerns}\BL{B-org-view}{Employer view}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] We split employers by whether most PME roles need on-site presence. Where they do, firms would require a much larger pay cut for any WFH: 52 against 3 per cent for one to two days, 60 against 25 for three to four days, 67 against 40 for fully remote. The WFH difference is statistically significant (p = .025) but not after correcting for the many splits we tested. % [M10, wtp_deck, employer_splits]
For the other arrangements we detect no difference: the compressed week 1 against 8 per cent, job sharing 24 against 23, part-time 32 against 36; staggered hours are higher where presence is needed, 22 against 7, but not significantly. The intervals are wide, 137 firms in one group, so we read this as no detectable difference, not as proof of none. % [employer_splits, p = .60]
So on-site needs mostly rule out location flexibility, not necessarily schedule or load. [Backup: tests; concerns.]}

\begin{frame}[t,label=M-concerns]{Employers who share a concern tend to ask for more}
  % F_org_concerns_m (scripts/fig_fwa_m.py; employer_splits.csv): difference in the pay cut required, firms that agree with the concern minus
  % firms that do not (points), all seven arrangements; filled = 95% interval excludes 0. Joint tests across all 7: productivity p = .25,
  % coordination .89, creativity .18, fairness .79; item-level p < .05 only for creativity (fully remote, staggered hours), not corrected for 28 items.
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_org_concerns_m}
  \Interp{Firms worried about creativity or productivity ask for more, notably for the compressed week.\\ But the differences are not statistically reliable.}
  \Backups{\BL{B-why-org-tests}{All tests}\BL{B-org-splits}{All splits}\BL{B-org-view}{Employer view}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Full deck only] Employers' main stated concerns are productivity, coordination, creativity and fairness across roles. Splitting firms by whether they agree with each concern, firms that do ask for more in 23 of 28 comparisons, on average 16 points more for the creativity concern, 10 for productivity, 5 for coordination and 3 for fairness. For WFH both groups ask for large cuts; for the compressed week and staggered hours, firms without the concern ask for nothing (about minus 3 per cent) while concerned firms ask for 15 to 22. But only three of the 28 differences are significant at 5 per cent, none after correcting for 28 tests, and the joint tests are not significant (p = .18 to .89). % [employer_splits]
Fairness is new here: it shows no difference at all. So concerns point the same way, but on-site needs are the more reliable guide. Back to PMEs: who values WFH less?}

  % F_why_pmes, true size 13.0 x 5.0 cm: flexible job's % of choices at equal pay, 95% CIs, by career belief
  % (QID51_1 agree 4-5, n = 455, vs others, n = 565) [M4]; legend "No expected penalty / Expected penalty".
  % 1-2 WFH days 52 [47, 57] vs 64 [60, 69]; 3-4 WFH days 52 vs 69; remote vs a 15-45 min commute 55 vs 72;

  % [S1] 1,020 PMEs, 4-21 Aug 2026; [M4] fully interacted model, equal-pay shares, 95% CIs
  \SourceNote{Penalty: expects flexible hours to hurt their career. }

% note facts: [M4] 52 vs 64, 1% level; [M5] compressed week 59 vs 58, p = .70, no detectable difference;
\note{[Short path] Surveyed PMEs who expect shorter or more flexible hours to hurt their career would give up about 2 per cent of pay for one to two WFH days, against 10 per cent for other PMEs; for three to four days, 2 against 14. The location difference is statistically significant (p = .002). For the compressed week we detect no difference (p = .15). % [M4, M5]
This is consistent with a visibility concern. We acknowledge that the career question was asked after the choices, and that part of the gap may be noisier answers. % [M6]
For firms and NTUC, appraisal by output could be part of any hybrid pilot.
Does fear of a career penalty also keep PMEs from asking? Barriers next.}

\note{[Short path] Three facts, on different bases. First, across all surveyed PMEs, 45 per cent expect shorter or more flexible hours to hurt their careers. % [M23, B5]
After accounting for who answered, parents of young children are somewhat more likely to expect a career penalty. % [M26] EB wording for NTUC, no number
Second, only three in ten surveyed junior PMEs are familiar with the Guidelines. % [D6]
Third, among PMEs who report a formal request, about four per cent report an outright refusal, or about seven per cent once arrangements that apply automatically are set aside, because the request item was partly misread: a selected group, so both are lower bounds. % [D7, D7b, D9]

\note{[Short path] So to the decision. We ask the partners to choose one measurement step and one bounded, voluntary practice pilot, and to nominate a lead for each. None requires a change to the Guidelines. % mandate: two-part decision; Lead decision 10
For the pilot, Option A is the most natural: SNEF could recruit volunteer firms to put compressed weeks on their written menu and test them, with NTUC co-designing safeguards, TAFEP providing guidance, and independent evaluation. The evidence is moderate, and operating costs are unmeasured. % [Q5, M16, M17, M19, M20]
Option B supports implementation: firms could review which tasks need presence, with Job Redesign+, and use flexi-load where fewer hours, not location, address the need. % [M10, Q10, P11, P5]
Option C, a three-to-four-day WFH pilot in roles without presence needs, is exploratory. % [M13, V6]
For measurement, Option D: MRSD, with NTUC and SNEF, could add why-not-request and partial-approval items where its surveys lack them; it adds no reporting duty for firms. % [P2, P3, B6, D9]
We close with three messages. % transition to M-conclusion
[Option letters link to B-optA to B-optD. Full deck: M-limits comes next.]}

\note{[Full deck only] We acknowledge six limits. The choices are stated, so rankings are firmer than levels. % [S5, V1-V5]
Respondents knew SNEF would use the results, which may invite strategic answers on both sides. % [S9]
The panels are online and unweighted, so shares describe surveyed PMEs and firms, not national rates. % [S4]
The employer task is a hiring choice, not a reply to a staff request, and does not measure operating costs. % [S2, S5]
Each side saw only 60 choice situations, with pay gaps of 17 to 33 per cent, so intervals are likely too narrow and employer cuts above 33 per cent are extrapolated. % [EB s9; S6, S6b]
The employer splits by role and concern were asked after the choices, so they remain preliminary associations. % [EB s9, M12]
And the request item was partly misread. % [D9, B6]
MOM, SNEF and NTUC could each support a next step for these limits. With that, the decision we ask for. % implication (who could act) and transition to M-conclusion
}

% 22. CONCLUSION: THE DECISION   [short path]
% ==========================================================================
\begin{frame}[t,label=M-conclusion]{The decision we ask of the partners}
  % Decision slide (mandate; COMMENTS slide 22): banner, then one take-away block with three robust
  % messages; the 490-PME detail is on B-followup; no "Thank you" here (M-thanks follows).
  % MANDATE: one bounded practice pilot; voluntary as on M-puzzle (fixer pass 7 Oct 2026: mom_ps-01 c, employer-04)
  \FrameTop
  \DecisionBanner{Decision sought today: one measurement step and one bounded, voluntary practice pilot, with a lead for each.}
  \vspace{0.20cm}% polish pass, 7 Oct 2026 (DESIGN_PLAN s2 W5): was 0.30 cm
  % Polish pass: no local font override in the block title; the restyled take-away card (preamble, G7) sets
  % the 11.5 pt bold Navy heading, the Navy top accent and the bold Navy numerals.
  \begin{alertblock}{Take-away messages}
    \begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.12cm}
      % [E1, E2] 7.4 and 9.5 -> about 7-10% of pay, status I (indicative); [S6] gaps shown 17-33%; not a pay cut (mandate)
      \item PMEs would accept \textbf{about 7--10\% lower pay} for hybrid work and about 15\% for fully remote work
      \item For WFH, employers ask for \textbf{12 to 34 points more}; only for the compressed week do the two sides agree
      \item Compressed week: \textbf{most promising common-ground test}; evidence moderate; operating costs unmeasured
    \end{enumerate}
  \end{alertblock}
  % mom_ps-01 (d): the proposed default, visible on the decision slide (Options D and A as on M-options)
  \Interp{We propose D (why-not and partial-approval items) and A (a compressed-week pilot).}
  \Backups{\BL{B-followup}{Follow-up} \BL{B-optD-items}{Survey items}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] Three messages. First, PMEs strongly prefer hybrid work: the model implies about seven to ten per cent of pay, an indicative value, not a case for lower pay. % [E1, E2, S6]
Second, the compressed week, the same hours over four longer days, is the most promising common-ground test: PMEs value it and we detect no hiring penalty, but the evidence is moderate and operating costs are unmeasured. % [S7, Q5, M19, M20]
Third, employers rank fully remote work last when they hire; that is a ranking, not a salary price. % [R10, Q3, Q16]
We acknowledge that these are stated choices, and the employer splits remain preliminary. % [S4, S5; EB s9 l.183]
The policy problem is therefore fit, not aggregate provision: which arrangement, for which role, and what blocks its use. A measurement step would show why PMEs who need an arrangement do not ask; a bounded pilot would show whether the compressed week works in practice. % [B6, P2]
For example, MRSD could lead the measurement step, and SNEF a voluntary compressed-week pilot with volunteer firms, with NTUC co-designing safeguards. % owners as on M-options; worker-08: the since-clause on career concern [M23, B5] dropped to keep the short path under 18:00
We ask the partners today to choose one measurement step and one bounded, voluntary practice pilot, and to nominate a lead for each. % decision request (same sentence closes both versions)
[30-second close: PMEs strongly prefer hybrid work, at an indicative seven to ten per cent of pay. The compressed week is the most promising common-ground test, with moderate evidence and unmeasured operating costs, so any pilot needs worker safeguards. Employers rank fully remote last in hiring; that is a ranking, not a price. We ask the partners today to choose one measurement step and one bounded, voluntary practice pilot, and to nominate a lead for each.]
[Follow-up design and consent scope: B-followup.]}

\note{[Full deck only] Three strands frame the study. First, worker valuations: abroad, a work-from-home option is worth about 4 to 8 per cent of pay; a 27-country survey puts Singapore at 4.8 per cent, from an online, mostly tertiary-educated sample. % [E16, L1]
Second, the employer side: a 2023 Polish working paper finds workers give up about 3 per cent of pay for remote or hybrid work, while employers expect a 21 per cent wage cut, mostly from expected productivity loss. A six-month trial found hybrid work cut quits by a third. % [R16, P7]
[If asked: the published version, ILR Review 2026, reports gaps of about 5 per cent of earnings for hybrid and 25 per cent for fully remote work.] % [R16] 5.2 and 24.6
Third, Singapore evidence is mostly descriptive. Our study complements this work by observing both sides on a common menu.
Next, a simple map for reading the results.}

% Note numbers: none. Information problem per MANDATE: a hiring reservation may reflect operating constraints,
% uncertainty or a candidate signal, and the hiring choices cannot separate them [S5; B-limits]
\note{[Short path] We read every result on this map. For each arrangement, we ask how much pay PMEs would give up for it, and how large a pay cut employers would require of a candidate who wants it. The difference is the gap.
Where the two are about the same and we detect no gap, there is common ground: firms and SNEF could make it easier to try.
Where the gap is moderate and depends on the role's tasks, firms can redesign jobs and test role by role.
Where PMEs would give up some pay but employers would require a much larger cut, the sides are far apart: pilot with volunteer firms before scaling.
A reservation may reflect real operating constraints, uncertainty, or what a request seems to signal; hiring choices cannot separate these; a pilot can show whether operating constraints materialise.
In any zone, career signals, redesign and missing information can block use.
Next, how we asked both sides. [Full deck: next, the two surveys.]}

% PI directive 6: a large illustrative choice task in the instrument's wording plus a three-step visual of

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-estimation]{How we turn choices into values}
  \FrameTop % first body token (centring; never a frame subtitle)

    % as on M-design

    % held rows (one value spanning A and B in the instrument) [S5]; the card's foot lines up with step 3's
    \node[deckheld,anchor=north west,inner xsep=0.08cm,inner ysep=0.04cm,minimum width=8.1cm,
      minimum height=0.89cm,text width=7.94cm] at (0,-4.23)

% note facts: [S5] six choices, employer version with two candidates; EB s3b: equal-pay share needs no pay
% slope, 50% = no preference, read within each side; [S6] 17 to 33 per cent; EB s9: magnitudes model-based;
% [V1-V5] stated choices predict direction and ranking well, levels less well
% implication, spoken: partners can rely on rankings; per cent of pay is a rough size, never a pay cut
\note{[Full deck only]
This is what a PME saw; employers saw two candidates. % [S5]
A statistical model estimates how pay and each arrangement shift the six choices. % [S5]
We report one number for each arrangement: a per cent of pay, the pay gap that makes the two options equally attractive. For PMEs it is the pay they would give up; for employers, the pay cut they would require of a candidate who wants it. % [EB s3b]
We acknowledge that no pair had equal pay and gaps ran from 17 to 33 per cent, so per cent of pay extrapolates. % [S6, EB s9]
MOM, SNEF and NTUC can rely on the rankings; per cent of pay is a rough size, never a proposed pay cut. % [V1-V5]
Next, what PMEs and firms do today.}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-groups]{No subgroup difference detected after correction}
  % F_groups_m (fig_v2.py, 13.0 x 5.0 cm; compressed-week column removed, ROUND5_SPEC s4):
  % PME equal-pay shares with 95% CIs by gender, age (19-39 / 40+) and caregiving (none / any),
  % for 1-2 WFH days, 3-4 WFH days and fully remote (vs a long commute); 50% reference [s3b].
  %   [Q14b] every plotted group's CI lies above 50% for the three WFH levels (lowest bound: men, 1-2 days, 51.2)
  %   [Q14] women 63/67/73% vs men 56/56/63% (location p = .047, nominal only); age p = .30; caregiving p = .53
  %   [E18] 198 pairwise contrasts, minimum BH q = .70; WTP joint tests p = .43 / .09 / .66
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_groups_m}
  % [E18, M7] null results are not equivalence (mandate: "Non-rejection is not equivalence")
  \Interp{Women and men, younger and older PMEs, and caregivers or not\\ all give up similar amounts; we find no clear differences.}
  % Note (polish pass 7 Oct 2026): the 95% CI convention (formerly in the figure's axis caption and this
  % source line, [s3b]); "Fully remote: vs a >45 min commute", moved out of the figure's column title
  % ([E3] main model: fully remote vs onsite with a long commute; [S8] long = >45 min); and the figure's
  % former "* Nominal" footnote, verbatim ([Q14] the starred p = .047 is nominal; [E18] 198 contrasts, BH).
  % [S1] 1,020 PMEs; [E18] BH correction over 198 contrasts; [M7] 7 primary splits
\end{frame}
\note{[Full deck only] In every group shown, the interval for the pay PMEs would give up for each WFH level lies above zero. % [Q14b]
None of 198 group contrasts survives correction for multiple testing, and we detect no differences by income, organisation type or tenure. % [E18, M7]
We acknowledge that no difference detected is not proof that groups are alike; mothers of young children are a small sample. % [M7] n = 108
Only the career-concern split stands out, as we saw earlier. % [M7, M4] a belief, not a demographic group
MOM, SNEF and NTUC could therefore treat PME demand for WFH as broad, not niche. Why, then, is the compressed week rare? % implication and transition to M-puzzle
}

  % T_robust_main (make_tables.py; do not edit): check | concern | result, 6 rows.

  % [R4, EB s9] version clusters, 60 pairs, staggered p = .15; [RB1, E11, R10]
  % rank pay model fits about as well, same ranking.
  % Printed in the shared main-table style, \MainTableStyle = 10 pt (ROUND5_SPEC s3: tables >= 9 pt;
  % polish pass G8, 7 Oct 2026; was 9 pt); \Tab would force the 8.5 pt backup \TableFont.
  \FrameTop % first body token (centring; never a frame subtitle)
  {\centering\MainTableStyle\input{tables/T_robust_main}\par}
  % [S6, S6b] pay gaps 17-33% by design (displayed about 16-34%; fixer pass 7 Oct 2026, editor-13): % of pay values are model-based;
  % [EB s9] 10 versions x 6 tasks = 60 distinct choice situations per survey;
  % [V1-V5] no cited validation study tests employer hiring choices (B-validity)
  \Interp{The rankings hold under every check;\\ the exact \% of pay values are less certain.}
  % [S1] 1,020 PMEs, 4-21 Aug 2026; [S2] 397 employer respondents (appended sample)
  \Backups{\BL{B-validity}{Validity} \BL{B-emp-robust}{Checks}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Full deck only] Which results survive changes to the analysis? % [E15, RB2]
Dropping implausible salaries, the top and bottom 1 per cent of income or inattentive respondents, or adding a position term, moves PME values by about one point of pay and employer values by up to three; the rankings hold. % [E15, RB2, E11, R10]
But the pay gaps shown were about 17 to 33 per cent, so values in per cent of pay are model-based. % [S6, S6b]
We acknowledge two further limits: each side saw only 60 choice situations, so intervals are likely too narrow, and no cited study validates employer hiring choices like these. % [EB s9; V1-V5]
MOM, SNEF and NTUC can therefore act on rankings; prices need a wave with small pay gaps. How do the zones compare? % implication (who could act) and transition to M-discussion
}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-puzzle-main]{The compressed week: valued, rarely offered}
  % F_puzzle_r5 (fig_r5.py, 13.0 x 5.0 cm), simplified to the puzzle only:
  %   PMEs choose the compressed-week job 58% of the time at equal pay (55-62) [Q5]
  %   offered by 26.5% of firms with a written FWA policy vs 9.7% without (association) [M17]
  %   take-up where available: about 1 in 3 (65 of 210 = 31.0%) [M22]
  % "compressed week" = the same total hours over four longer days [S7]
  \FrameTop
  \FigC{F_puzzle_r5}
  % pilot framing: COMMENTS slide 16; mandate (voluntary, evaluated; not costless)
  \Interp{PMEs would give up about 7\% of pay for it, yet few firms offer it.\\ A voluntary, evaluated pilot is the next step.}
  % Note (polish pass 7 Oct 2026): the figure's former footnote ("+ All respondents / excluding one online
  % panel. Surveyed samples, unweighted.") with the deck's one dagger wording \DgShort [S1, S2];
  % [M20] cheaper option in 83.2% of PME pairs (1,502/1,805) and 90.8% of employer pairs (327/360)
  \Backups{\BL{B-puzzle}{Offering} \BL{B-pilot}{Pilot checklist}}
\end{frame}
\note{[Short path] PMEs would give up about 7 per cent of pay for the compressed week and employers would require about the same, yet only about one surveyed firm in six offers it. % [E5, R5, M16]
Firms with a written FWA policy offer it more often, 21 against 9 per cent, though a policy may follow offering rather than lead it. % [M17] association
Where it is available, about one surveyed PME in three takes it up. % [M22]
We acknowledge that the design usually made it the cheaper option, and a hiring experiment cannot measure rostering, fatigue or service coverage. % [M20]
So the case is for a voluntary, evaluated pilot, not a roll-out: SNEF could recruit volunteer firms to put it on their written menu, with NTUC co-designing safeguards. What happens when PMEs ask? % implication (who could act) and transition to M-barriers
}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-talent]{What FWAs offer firms seeking talent}
  \FrameTop
  % polish pass (BKb): list frames with room use the 9.5 pt backup body (as the Body macro), items 0.08 cm apart

        \item PMEs value hybrid at \ap 7--10\% of pay, a compressed week \ap 7\% (indicative)

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-partners]{What each partner has said}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}

    % [P3] MOM's frictions reading; [P18] COS 2026 too-blunt remark (FACTCHECK F31)
    \item \textbf{MOM:} reads the need-request gap as ``frictions \ldots\ rather than employer resistance''; at COS 2026 called a proposal to make the Guidelines law, and FWAs a presumptive right for parents of young children, ``too blunt'', as business needs differ by industry and role.
    % [P9b] SNEF three principles, 23 Apr 2024; SUSS x SNEF: 367 firms, Sep 2024, 81% prepared
    \item \textbf{SNEF:} endorses the Guidelines on three principles: outcomes stay the employer's prerogative; FWAs must not harm productivity or service quality; not every role suits every FWA. SUSS$\times$SNEF (367 firms, 2024): 81\% felt prepared.
    % [P12] NTUC in MOM's release of 16 Apr 2024; [P8] online survey, Nov-Dec 2025, N = 1,508; 36% primary concern, most-cited
    \item \textbf{NTUC:} FWA access is often the main consideration for caregivers, women and senior workers in staying in or returning to work. PAP Women's Wing--NTUC survey (online, N = 1,508; sampling not published): 36\% named stigma their primary concern in requesting an FWA (most cited).
  \end{itemize}
  \SourceNote{\textbf{Sources:} MRSD (2026); MOM COS 2026 (3 Mar 2026); SNEF statement (23 Apr 2024); SUSS--SNEF (2025); MOM release (16 Apr 2024); PAP Women's Wing, NTUC (Mar 2026).}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-legal]{FWA request rules elsewhere}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}
  % Verified wording from FACTCHECK_REPORT F28 F31 F32 F33 (slide_patches.md s1); [P1, P17] Singapore; [P20] foreign law; [P18, P19] too blunt, acrimonious
  % Declutter: the full P17 wording (could include educational workshops) stays on B-guidelines.
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.10cm}
    \item \textbf{Singapore:} tripartite guidelines on the process, not the outcome; TAFEP takes an educational approach.
    % [P20] GB: Employment Rights Act 2025 changes due in 2027, not yet in force (DBT timeline, 25 Sep 2026)
    \item \textbf{Great Britain:} statutory right to request from day one (since Apr 2024); decision within 2 months; refusal only on eight listed business reasons; a tribunal if a request is not handled reasonably, not merely if refused. Employment Rights Act 2025 changes due in 2027.
    % [P20] Australia, Fair Work Act 2009 ss65-65C; New Zealand, Employment Relations Act 2000 Part 6AA; Workgroup s2.4.1
    \item \textbf{Australia:} eligible employees (e.g.\ parents, carers, 55+); written reply within 21 days; refusal only on reasonable business grounds; the Fair Work Commission can arbitrate and, as a last resort, order it granted. \textbf{New Zealand:} any employee; reply within 1 month; eight listed grounds; disputes cover process only. In both, most requests are informal.
    % [P19] acrimonious, Workgroup s3.2.2; [P18] COS 2026 too blunt, with its full object
    \item \textbf{Why guidelines here:} the Workgroup judged legislation risks an acrimonious workplace culture; at COS 2026, MOM called legislating the Guidelines, with a presumptive FWA right for parents of young children, too blunt.
  \end{itemize}
  % TODO(PI): re-check the UK DBT timeline (Employment Rights Act 2025) in Jan 2027 (EB P20, s14)
  % Check date: EB P20 sources GOV.UK updated 5 Oct 2026, DBT timeline 25 Sep 2026; EB s14 fact-check log, 6 Oct 2026
  \SourceNote{\textbf{Sources:} MOM COS 2026, FAQ (Jun 2026); Workgroup report (2024); gov.uk/flexible-working; Fair Work Act 2009 ss65--65C; Employment Relations Act 2000 (NZ) Part 6AA. Checked 6 Oct 2026.}
  \BackToTwo{M-options}{Options}{M-question}{Question}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-intl]{Evidence elsewhere: concerns and trials}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9.5}{11.6}\selectfont}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.14cm}
    % [R16, L1] IZA DP 2023: 2.9% vs 21%, pooled; ILR Review 2026: 5.2% hybrid, 24.6% fully remote; Lead decision 4 (EB s14)
    \item \textbf{Poland, two-sided experiment:} workers give up 2.9\% of pay for remote work; employers expect a 21\% wage cut, mostly for lost productivity (Lewandowski et al., IZA DP 16041, 2023; hybrid and fully remote pooled). ILR Review (2026) version: gaps \ap 5\% (hybrid), 25\% (fully remote).
    % [P7, V6] six-month RCT, 1,612 graduates; quits down by a third; promotions n.s. over two years; managers -2.6% to +1.0%
    \item \textbf{Randomised hybrid trial} (two days a week; 1,612 graduates, one Chinese firm): quits fell by one-third over six months; over two years, reviews were unaffected and promotions showed no statistically significant difference; managers' productivity view: $-$2.6\% to +1.0\% (Bloom, Han \& Liang, Nature 2024).
    % [P4] employer-reported shares, mid-2024
    \item \textbf{Singapore firms offering scheduled FWAs:} 69.5\% report better engagement, 65.9\% retention, 59.9\% productivity (employer-reported, mid-2024; MRSD).
    % [L1] Barrero, Bloom & Davis 2023; Emanuel & Harrington 2024 (FACTCHECK F25)
    \item \textbf{Fully remote:} evidence is mixed and job-dependent; several studies find lower productivity, partly reflecting who selects into remote jobs (Barrero, Bloom \& Davis 2023; Emanuel \& Harrington 2024).
  \end{itemize}
  % [P7] co-author disclosure
  \SourceNote{Other settings; read as context. Trip.com trial: co-author James Liang co-founded and chairs Trip.com.}
  \BackToTwo{B-framework}{Framework}{M-discussion}{Discussion}
\end{frame}

% ==========================================================================
% Method
% ==========================================================================
% Round 5: receives the equations from M-estimation (PI directive 6; ROUND5_SPEC s5). The employer
% free-slope check is NOT available: stated as pending, never as run (EB s9; mandate).
\begin{frame}[t,label=B-methods]{Equations and inference}
  % EB s3b: conditional logit per side, log salary plus one indicator per arrangement level; SEs clustered by respondent
  \FrameTop % first body token (centring; never a frame subtitle)
  {\centering\fontsize{10}{12}\selectfont $U_{ijt}=\beta_w\ln w_{ijt}+\sum_k\beta_k x_{kijt}+\varepsilon_{ijt}$\par}
  \vspace{0.04cm}
  {\centering\color{Muted}\fontsize{8.5}{10.2}\selectfont Conditional logit per side; SEs clustered by respondent.\par}
  \vspace{0.08cm}
  \begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Pay given up: $100\,[1-\exp(-\beta_k/\beta_w)]$}
      % [S6] gaps shown 17-33%; [RB1] a which-paid-more indicator fits about as well on both sides; EB s3 header
      {\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont\RaggedRight For PMEs ($\beta_w>0$), the pay they would give up for $k$; for employers ($\beta_w<0$), the pay cut they would require of a candidate who wants $k$. Positive = a pay cut. Indicative: gaps shown were 17--33\%, and a which-paid-more indicator fits about as well.\par}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Gap: employers' cut $-$ PMEs' give-up}
      % EB s3b invlogit, no salary coefficient, 50% = no preference; EB s10 seven arrangements: at most 1 point (employers), 3 (PMEs);
      % fixer pass 7 Oct 2026 (fact_audit WRONG 4): the scope, for the seven arrangements, is now on the slide (culture moves 4.9, Q9)
      {\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont\RaggedRight Positive = friction. Its 95\% interval combines both sides' delta-method standard errors (independent samples). Employer cuts above 33\% go beyond the pay gaps shown, so gaps are indicative.\par}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \vspace{0.06cm}
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.03cm}
    % EB s9: 10 versions x 6 tasks = 60; [E18] 198 PME contrasts; [M7] 7 PME mechanism splits; [M12] 20 employer splits
    \item \textbf{Tests:} 60 choice situations per side, so intervals may be too narrow. Benjamini--Hochberg by family: 198 PME contrasts, 7 PME mechanisms, 11 employer split tests.
    % [M8] free-slope tests added after the pre-specified convention; EB s9: no employer free-slope check yet for presence and creativity
    \item \textbf{Pay slopes:} group splits use a separate pay slope for each group. Employers' role and concern items were asked after the choices, so these splits are preliminary associations.
    % [RB2] PME arrangement values move at most 2 points; [E15]; EB s9: task-1 coding moves remote by about 0.5 point
    \item \textbf{Checks:} without outliers, the top and bottom 1\% of income or same-side respondents, or with a position term, PME values move $\le$1.3 points and employer values $\le$2.5. To fix: task-1 coding (\ap 0.5 point, remote).
  \end{itemize}
  % [L1] McFadden (1974), conditional logit (EB L1 since the fixer pass, 7 Oct 2026; fact_audit UNTRACED 4)
  \SourceNote{$i$ respondent, $j$ option, $t$ task; $w$ pay shown; $x_k$ arrangement level $k$. McFadden (1974).}
  \BackToTwo{B-estimation}{Estimation}{B-framework}{Framework}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-pilot]{A compressed-week pilot: checklist}
  % Fixer pass 7 Oct 2026, merging verified persona fixes: worker-02 (pay and leave unchanged; collective
  % agreements; voluntary for each employee, reversible without penalty; care hours; appraisal by output;
  % worker data only with consent; stop criteria agreed with the partners), employer-06 (for firms and staff;
  % fairness to staff who cannot take part; operating costs and coverage as outcomes), editor-06 (comparison
  % group), mom_ps-07 (bounds to agree), worker-07 (eligibility and fairness). Items at 9 pt and columns 0.34/0.24/0.39 (polish pass: 0.32/0.27/0.37):
  % at 10 pt (worker-02's fallback) the frame still overflowed by 1.28 cm in layout_sim; this is a backup frame.
  % [S7] compressed week = same total hours over fewer, longer days; never a shorter week
  % [B1] fairness to staff who cannot have FWAs: 23%, the top challenge at 200 or fewer staff (28%); [B2] 50% agree
  % it is unfair to offer FWAs to PMEs when frontline staff cannot have them (not printed)
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9}{11}\selectfont}
  \begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
    \begin{column}{0.32\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Design}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.04cm}
        \item Same hours, four longer days; pay and leave unchanged
        \item Legal, contract and collective-agreement review
        \item Voluntary for firms and staff; reversible without penalty
        \item Eligibility; fairness to staff who cannot join
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.27\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Safeguards}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.04cm}
        \item Service and coverage plan
        \item Fatigue, safety and care hours
        \item Workload spillovers
        \item Appraisal by output, not presence
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.37\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{Evaluation}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.04cm}
        \item Outcomes: output, operating costs, coverage, retention, take-up, worker experience
        \item Stop and scale criteria agreed with the partners in advance
        \item Independent evaluation with a comparison group; worker data only with consent, never for appraisal
        % Governance: publication rule not yet agreed (mandate; EB G0)
        \item Publication rule: [PI to confirm]
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-tgfwar]{What we can say about the Guidelines}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9.5}{11.6}\selectfont}
  \begin{columns}[T,onlytextwidth]
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{What we observe (2026)}
      % [D6, D6x, D7, D7b, D5x, D10]
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.08cm}
        \item Familiar: 55\% of surveyed PMEs, 29\% of juniors, 58\% of employers
        \item Of PMEs reporting a formal request, 4\% were declined (7\%, stricter definition): a lower bound
        \item More FWAs came via company policy (43\%) than individual request (30\%)
        \item Aware firms with a written policy got more requests (68\% vs 19\%; an association)
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
      \PanelTitle{Navy}{What we cannot say}
      \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.08cm}
        \item Whether the Guidelines changed outcomes (no before-and-after)
        \item National rates (unweighted panels)

\OptionFrame{B-optA}{Option A: put compressed weeks on the menu and test them}
  {\textbf{Zone:} A, common ground\quad\textbf{Strength:} moderate; operating costs unmeasured}
  {
   % [M16] 20.8% offer; [M17] 26.5 vs 9.7, an association; [M20] 83.2 and 90.8
   PMEs would give up about 7\% of pay for it; employers would require about 7\% (wide interval): no detectable gap. 1 surveyed firm in 6 offers it, more often with a written policy (21\% vs 9\%). It was the cheaper option in 83\% (PME) and 91\% (employer) of its pairs.}
  {% W5 M-options owner: SNEF with volunteer firms; NTUC co-designs safeguards; TAFEP guidance
   \textbf{SNEF}, with volunteer member firms: put it on the written menu and test it in a bounded, evaluated pilot (\hyperlink{B-pilot}{\textcolor{Navy}{checklist}}). \textbf{NTUC:} co-design safeguards. \textbf{TAFEP:} guidance.}
  {% [P21] TAFEP, IHRP and SNEF resources (V-09)
   % TODO(PI): confirm the SNEF guide's exact title with SNEF (FACTCHECK V-09)
   TAFEP and IHRP resources; SNEF guidance on FWA requests.}
  {% [S7] the same total hours over four longer days
   Not shorter hours (same hours, four longer days), a mandate or a case for lower pay; not shown to be costless.}
  {% [D2x] take-up 31 [33]
   Output, coverage, rostering, fatigue; take-up where available (31\%).}
  {\SourceNote{Associations, not causes: a policy may follow offering. Hiring choices do not measure operating costs.}%
   \BackToTwo{M-options}{Options}{B-puzzle-main}{Puzzle}}

\OptionFrame{B-optB}{Option B: fit arrangements to the role, with flexi-load}
  {\textbf{Zone:} B, depends on the role\quad\textbf{Strength:} moderate; preliminary associations}
  {% [Q10, M10] 27 vs 48 (appended); [Q10b] 50 (appended); [Q10c] p = .002 vs 1-2 days; [M12] p = .006, q = .058 over 20 splits; EB s9 l.183 one pay slope, free-slope check pending
   % [M13] part-time 35 where neither presence need nor creativity concern
   Where most roles need presence, firms would require a pay cut of about 52\% for 1--2 WFH days (3\% elsewhere), against about 1\% for a compressed week. Presence: p = .025 (q = .14 over 11 split tests; preliminary).}
  {% [P11] Job Redesign+ up to 70% of qualifying costs for SMEs, 50% for others; PTRG under review for flexi-load
   % [Q10c] say "a compressed week may fit where WFH does not" (fixer pass 7 Oct 2026, employer-11; fact_audit s3 item 6)
   \textbf{Firms}, with SNEF: review which tasks need presence; a compressed week may fit where WFH does not; use flexi-load where fewer hours, not location, address the need. Job Redesign+: up to 70\% of qualifying costs for SMEs, 50\% for others. \textbf{MOM:} PTRG review.}
  {% [P11] EWTP from Mar 2026, linked to FWAs at COS 2026
   EWTP (Mar 2026), linked by MOM to FWAs.}
  {Not one-size-fits-all; not a quota.}
  {% [B1] fairness top challenge at 200 or fewer staff, 28%; [P5] COS 2026 speech: under half who needed part-time got it, 2024
   Fairness to staff without FWAs (top challenge, $\le$200 staff); part-time access (COS 2026: under half who needed it got it).}
  {\SourceNote{Associations; asked after the choices. \hyperlink{B-flexiload}{\textcolor{Navy}{Flexi-load}}.}%
   \BackToTwo{M-options}{Options}{M-where}{Reservations}}

% [S7] 3-4 WFH days is a tested attribute level; W5 M-options row C
\OptionFrame{B-optC}{Option C: a 3--4-day WFH pilot where roles allow}
  {\textbf{Zone:} C, far apart\quad\textbf{Strength:} exploratory}
  {
   Employers would require pay cuts of about 36\% for 3--4 WFH days and 49\% for fully remote work (PMEs would give up 10\% and 15\%). Fully remote draws about 61\% where firms worry that creativity suffers apart, against 36\% elsewhere (a weak association, p = .14; preliminary). Abroad, a six-month hybrid trial cut quits by a third.}
  {% W5 M-options owner: volunteer firms; independent evaluation; Lead decision 10: roles without presence needs
   \textbf{Volunteer firms}, with SNEF and NTUC: a 3--4-day WFH pilot in roles without presence needs; outcomes agreed upfront; independent evaluation; stop criteria set in advance. Convenor, funding and publication rule: for the partners.}
  {% [V6] managers' perceived productivity effect -2.6% to +1.0%
   Trials abroad (managers' productivity view: $-$2.6\% to +1.0\%).}
  {% [L1] fully remote evidence mixed (FACTCHECK F25)
   Not a push for fully remote work (mixed evidence; some studies find lower productivity); not a mandate; no pay change.}
  {Output, retention, collaboration; whether managers' concerns are borne out.}
  {\SourceNote{Bloom, Han \& Liang (2024); Barrero, Bloom \& Davis (2023); Emanuel \& Harrington (2024).}%
   \BackToTwo{M-options}{Options}{M-meet}{Two sides}}

\OptionFrame{B-optD}{Option D: why-not-request and partial-approval items}
  {\textbf{Zone:} all (measurement)\quad\textbf{Strength:} gap documented}
  {% [P2] no administrative counts; [P3] 18.5% made a formal request, data for 2024; [D9] misread item; [B6] no why-not item
   % [D7] 4.4 [7.2] declined, 32 [42] partly; [D7b] lower bound; [M23] 44.6 [37.1]; [M27] more formal requests, not fewer
   % fixer pass 7 Oct 2026 (mom_ps-02 b): [P3] MOM publishes request rates; [B6] our survey had no why-not item; whether MRSD's
   % questionnaire already asks why is a PI gate before the meeting (REPORT.md)
   Firms need not report requests to MOM; in MOM's survey, 18.5\% of those needing an FWA made a formal request (data for 2024). MOM publishes request rates, not reasons; our survey had no why-not item, and our request item was partly misread. Of PMEs reporting a request, about 4\% were declined (a lower bound) and 32\% partly approved. 45\% expect a career penalty; it goes with more requests, not fewer.}
  {% W5 M-options owner: MRSD checks the items against its survey, with NTUC and SNEF (fixer pass 7 Oct 2026, mom_ps-02);
   % COMMENTS slide 20: first deliverable restricted to the two items
   \textbf{MOM (MRSD)}, with NTUC and SNEF: check its survey, then add the items not yet asked: why those who need an FWA do not ask, and whether a request was approved in full, with changes, or declined (\hyperlink{B-optD-items}{\textcolor{Navy}{draft}}).}
  {MOM's employee survey; partners' outreach channels.}
  {Not a new reporting duty for firms; not an evaluation of the Guidelines.}
  {% [D6] junior 29 [25] familiar; [P15] about 6% of FWA users reported a setback in 2025, experience not expectation
   Partial approvals; junior PMEs' awareness (29\% familiar); expected penalty vs MOM's reported setbacks (\ap 6\% of FWA users, 2025).}
  {\SourceNote{Surveyed samples, unweighted.}%

\begin{frame}[t,label=B-language]{Public wording}
  \FrameTop
  \setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\fontsize{9.5}{11.4}\selectfont}
  \PanelTitle{Navy}{We say}
  \begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0.02cm}
    % [E1, E2] about 7-10, indicative; never a pay cut
    \item PMEs strongly prefer hybrid work: about 7--10\% of pay, indicative, never a pay cut.
    % [Q1, Q2, Q5] about six in ten; EB s3b plain-English reading, choices not people
    \item Employers would require larger pay cuts than PMEs would give up for most arrangements; for the compressed week the two are about equal.
    % [R5, Q5] no detectable penalty; [R10, R12] fully remote ranked last (both hold in the appended sample)
    \item Hiring: no detectable gap for a compressed week; fully remote draws the largest cut (a ranking).
    % [M10] presence and creativity contrasts; EB s9: free-slope check pending
    \item Reservations: 1--2 WFH days where most roles need presence; remote with the creativity concern; preliminary (asked after the choices).
    % Lead decision 2; mandate: compressed-week conclusion wording
    \item Compressed week: most promising common-ground test; evidence moderate; operating costs unmeasured.
    % [M23] more than a third; [D7, D7b] lower bound
    \item Over a third of surveyed PMEs expect a career penalty; refusals are a lower bound.
  \end{itemize}
  \vspace{0.06cm}
  \PanelTitle{Navy}{We avoid}
  \Body{Pay values as a proposed pay cut, or employer cut sizes as a price (read the ranking); a request rate; ``easy'', ``low cost'', ``no cost'', ``indifferent''; associations or nulls as causes or proof; Guidelines effects on provision, requests or approvals.}
  \BackToTwo{M-meet}{Two sides}{M-conclusion}{Conclusion}
\end{frame}
